questions.stem: A new GitHub Actions job runs `claude "Review this PR for bugs"`. The step produces no output and hangs until the 60-minute job timeout kills it. Locally, the same command opens an interactive session. What is the fix?

options.text: Set `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=1` in the job environment, so Claude Code detects that no terminal is attached and exits after responding.
options.why: This isn't a real Claude Code setting, which makes it an invented distractor.

options.text: Run it in print mode: `claude -p "Review this PR for bugs"`.
options.why: Print mode runs once and exits, which is what CI needs.

options.text: Add `--batch` so the review is submitted through the batch pipeline and the step returns immediately.
options.why: This flag doesn't exist, and batch processing would be wrong for a PR check anyway.

options.text: Allocate a pseudo-terminal with `script -q /dev/null` around the command, so the interactive session can start normally.
options.why: This hack still runs an interactive session that waits for input.

questions.explanation: `-p`/`--print` is the non-interactive mode for scripts and CI. Watch out for made-up flags among the distractors.

questions.stem: A downstream script turns review findings into inline PR comments. It needs reliably parseable output with the fields `file`, `line`, `severity` and `message`. Last week, 4% of runs broke the parser. What should the CI invocation use?

options.text: Ask for findings as a Markdown table, and parse the table rows with a regular expression in the posting script.
options.why: Regex-parsing free-form output is brittle, which is what broke last week.

options.text: Keep the text output, but add a retry that re-runs the review whenever the parser fails, up to three attempts.
options.why: This treats the symptom, wasting runs and adding latency.

options.text: Write the findings to a file named in CLAUDE.md, and have the posting script read that file after the run.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is memory, not an output channel, and file format remains unenforced.

options.text: `claude -p` with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`, so the output is structured and matches the expected shape.
options.why: Structured output flags make CI output reliably parseable.

questions.explanation: In CI, combine `-p` with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` to get structured, validated output.

questions.stem: The CI reviewer runs on every push to an open PR. A PR with 9 pushes received the same 12 findings 9 times, and the author muted the bot. What is the best fix?

options.text: Include the previous findings or existing comments in the prompt, and ask for new or still-unresolved issues only.
options.why: Supplying prior findings avoids duplicate reports.

options.text: Trigger the review only when the PR is first opened or marked ready, and skip later pushes to avoid repetition.
options.why: New pushes would go unreviewed, including fixes that introduce new bugs.

options.text: Delete all previous bot comments at the start of each run, so only the latest run's findings are visible.
options.why: This loses history, and it still re-notifies the author with the same findings.

options.text: Deduplicate in the posting script by hashing each finding's message text, and skip any message seen before.
options.why: Model wording varies between runs, so hashes rarely match, and the model still spends effort on old issues.

questions.explanation: Give CI reviewers the prior findings so that they report only what is new.

questions.stem: The test-suggestion step frequently proposes tests that already exist, for example a "null input" test for a function whose test file already covers it. Developers have started to ignore all its suggestions. What should change?

options.text: Ask the model to suggest only "non-obvious" tests, on the assumption that existing tests cover the obvious cases.
options.why: This is a guess about coverage, and it may skip genuinely missing obvious tests.

options.text: Limit the step to three suggestions per PR, so that duplicates are less noticeable and suggestions stay reviewable.
options.why: Duplicates would still appear, just fewer of them.

options.text: Give the model the existing relevant tests or a coverage summary, and request tests only for uncovered behaviour.
options.why: The model can't avoid duplicating tests it hasn't seen.

options.text: Filter suggestions after generation by fuzzy-matching their names against existing test names in the repo.
options.why: Name matching is unreliable, because similar names can test different behaviour and vice versa.

questions.explanation: Provide existing tests as context to avoid duplicate test suggestions.

questions.stem: In one CI job, Claude generates a fix for a failing test and then, in the same session, reviews its own fix before auto-committing it. The reviews approve 98% of fixes, yet humans later revert 15% of them. What is the architectural problem?

options.text: The review prompt is too lenient. Adding a strict checklist of failure modes would make the same session more critical.
options.why: A checklist helps a little, but the bias comes from the shared context, not the prompt wording.

options.text: The reviewer shares the generator's context and reasoning, so it is biased toward approval. Use an independent instance.
options.why: An independent review instance catches issues that self-review misses.

options.text: The fix and review should both run with extended thinking, so the session reasons more carefully about each fix.
options.why: The same context still has the same blind spots.

options.text: The job should run the full test suite instead of the review, since tests are objective and reviews are not.
options.why: Tests are valuable, but they don't replace independent review of design and correctness concerns.

questions.explanation: Self-review is weak because the model retains its generation reasoning. Use separate instances for review.

questions.stem: Claude Code in CI ignores the repo's conventions (error-handling style, banned dependencies), although developers' local sessions follow them. The conventions currently live in a wiki page that developers paste into their personal memory. Where should they live?

options.text: In a repository secret that the CI workflow injects into the prompt through an environment variable on each run.
options.why: This duplicates the source of truth and works only in CI.

options.text: In each developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and the CI runner's home directory is populated from a shared template.
options.why: This is fragile duplication, and personal memory isn't the right home for team rules.

options.text: In the committed project CLAUDE.md and `.claude/rules/`, which Claude Code loads from the checkout in CI and locally.
options.why: Project memory supplies context to CI invocations too.

options.text: In the CI job's prompt string, maintained alongside the workflow YAML file, so CI and local runs can differ as needed.
options.why: This creates drift between local and CI behaviour, and a second source of truth.

questions.explanation: Committed project CLAUDE.md gives CI runs the same project context as local runs.

questions.stem: About 60% of the bot's comments are style nits or false positives, and developers have started ignoring it, including its security findings. The prompt says "Be conservative and only report important issues." What is the most effective change?

options.text: Add "only report findings you are at least 90% confident about", so low-confidence speculation is filtered out.
options.why: Confidence filtering relies on poorly calibrated self-assessment.

options.text: Cap the bot at three comments per PR, ranked by its own assessment of importance.
options.why: This might drop real security findings while keeping nits.

options.text: Switch to a larger model, which is better at judging what counts as "important" without detailed instructions.
options.why: It doesn't fix the underspecified criteria.

options.text: Replace it with explicit criteria: what to report (security, correctness, data loss) and what to skip (linter-covered style), with examples.
options.why: Explicit criteria reduce false positives more reliably than vague caution.

questions.explanation: Specific, categorical criteria beat "be conservative" or confidence thresholds for precision.

questions.stem: Triage shows that most false positives come from one category, "possible performance issue". Security findings are accurate and valued. Rewriting the performance criteria will take about two weeks. What is the best immediate step?

options.text: Temporarily disable the performance category to rebuild trust, while its criteria and examples are refined offline.
options.why: False positives erode trust in all findings, so removing the noisy category protects the valuable ones.

options.text: Keep the category, but label its comments "low confidence", so developers can choose to skip them.
options.why: The noise remains, and trust keeps eroding.

options.text: Pause the whole bot for two weeks until all categories have been revised, then relaunch with a clean slate.
options.why: This loses the valued security findings during that time.

options.text: Keep everything as-is, and run a developer workshop on how to interpret and filter the bot's output.
options.why: This pushes the system's precision problem onto developers.

questions.explanation: False positives erode trust, so temporarily disabling a noisy category is a legitimate, proportionate move.

questions.stem: The bot is inconsistent about severity. The same SQL string-concatenation pattern is rated "critical" in one PR and "minor" in another, which confuses developers about what blocks a merge. What improves consistency the most?

options.text: Run each review three times, and take the most common severity for each finding to smooth out the variation.
options.why: This is costly and doesn't define what each severity means.

options.text: Define each severity level with explicit criteria and concrete code examples, such as user input concatenated into SQL as critical.
options.why: Concrete severity definitions anchored with examples drive consistent classification.

options.text: Drop severity and let developers decide what matters, since the bot's ratings are unreliable anyway.
options.why: Severity is needed to decide what blocks a merge.

options.text: Add the instruction "be consistent with severity across reviews" to the prompt, near the output format section.
options.why: This is vague guidance with nothing to anchor it.

questions.explanation: Severity criteria with concrete code examples produce consistent ratings.

questions.stem: The bot flags the team's intentional use of `any` in generated API-client files as a type-safety issue. It does this even though a comment in the prompt says generated code is exempt. It also catches real `any` misuse in hand-written code. Which technique best teaches the distinction?

options.text: Exclude all files under `generated/` from review with a path filter, so they are never sent to the model.
options.why: This is reasonable for generated code, but it doesn't teach the distinction where the pattern is ambiguous.

options.text: Add 30–50 examples of correct and incorrect `any` usage drawn from across the codebase to the prompt.
options.why: This bloats the prompt. A few targeted examples are more effective.

options.text: Add 2–4 contrasting few-shot examples (a generated client vs hand-written code), each with its reasoning.
options.why: Few-shot examples with reasoning are the right tool for ambiguous distinctions.

options.text: Tell the bot never to flag `any`, and rely on the TypeScript compiler's strict mode to catch misuse.
options.why: The bot would miss genuine issues that strict mode configuration doesn't catch.

questions.explanation: Use a few targeted examples (2–4) for ambiguous cases, and show the reasoning that separates acceptable patterns from real issues.

questions.stem: Findings come back in inconsistent shapes. Some include line numbers, some include suggested fixes, and some have neither, which makes them hard to act on. Alongside schema enforcement, what is the most effective prompt-level improvement?

options.text: Ask for "detailed, actionable findings" and explain that developers need enough information to fix each issue.
options.why: This is vague and doesn't show the expected format.

options.text: Include few-shot examples showing the exact format of a finding: location, issue, severity and suggested fix.
options.why: Examples that demonstrate the format improve consistency.

options.text: Lower the temperature to 0, so the model formats findings identically every time.
options.why: This reduces variation, but it doesn't define the target format.

options.text: Post-process the findings, filling in missing line numbers by searching the diff for each finding's message text.
options.why: This is fragile repair after the fact.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples should demonstrate the desired output format as well as the reasoning.

questions.stem: An engineering manager wants to move all CI model calls to the Message Batches API to save 50%. That covers (a) the blocking pre-merge review on each PR and (b) the nightly technical-debt summary across repos. What is the correct evaluation?

options.text: Move both. Most batches finish within an hour, so the pre-merge delay is acceptable for a 50% saving.
options.why: There is no latency guarantee, and a batch can take up to 24 hours, which could block merges for a day.

options.text: Move neither, because batch results come back unordered and can't be reliably matched to PRs or repositories.
options.why: `custom_id` correlates results with requests.

options.text: Move only the pre-merge review, since it runs most often and therefore produces most of the savings.
options.why: This is exactly the job that can't tolerate batch latency.

options.text: Move only (b); batches can take up to 24 hours with no latency SLA, which can't work for a blocking pre-merge check.
options.why: Match the API to the latency requirements.

questions.explanation: The Batches API is for non-blocking, latency-tolerant jobs. Use `custom_id` to correlate results.

questions.stem: The nightly debt job submits 3,000 requests in one batch. When it completes, 41 requests have failed, mostly with transient errors, and the morning report is due at 08:00. What should the job do next?

options.text: Find the failed requests by `custom_id` and resubmit only those.
options.why: Resubmit only the failures, correlated through `custom_id`.

options.text: Resubmit the entire 3,000-request batch, so the report is generated from one consistent run.
options.why: This wastes cost and time on the 2,959 successes and risks missing the deadline.

options.text: Publish the report without the 41 repositories, since 98.6% coverage is acceptable for a nightly summary.
options.why: This leaves silent coverage gaps. At minimum the gaps should be retried or annotated.

options.text: Switch the job to synchronous API calls permanently, so failures are retried immediately and never accumulate.
options.why: This loses the 50% saving over a small failure rate.

questions.explanation: Batch best practices: correlate with `custom_id`, retry failures selectively, and refine prompts on a sample before full runs.

questions.stem: A 22-file PR receives a single-pass review that misses obvious bugs in some files and makes contradictory claims about others, such as calling a function both unused and over-called. Which restructuring is best?

options.text: Use a model with a larger context window, so the whole diff and surrounding files fit comfortably in one pass.
options.why: A bigger window doesn't fix diluted attention.

options.text: Run the single pass three times, and keep only findings that appear in at least two of the runs.
options.why: Consensus filtering suppresses real but intermittently detected bugs.

options.text: Review each file (or small group) in a focused pass, then run a separate pass for cross-file interactions.
options.why: This avoids attention dilution while still catching cross-file issues.

options.text: Require PRs to touch at most five files, and have the bot refuse to review larger PRs until they are split.
options.why: This pushes the architecture problem onto developers.

questions.explanation: Multi-pass review means per-file local passes plus a cross-file integration pass.

questions.stem: The team wants to auto-post high-certainty findings and send uncertain ones to a human triage queue that handles about 30 items a day. Which TWO elements are needed for this routing to be trustworthy? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Have the reviewer output a confidence value per finding, as a structured field in its schema.
options.why: Per-finding confidence enables routing.

options.text: Calibrate the thresholds on a labelled set of past findings (true and false positives) before relying on them.
options.why: Uncalibrated self-reported confidence is unreliable, and calibration makes it usable.

options.text: Use the model's raw confidence directly, since recent models are well calibrated on code-review tasks.
options.why: Raw self-reported confidence isn't reliably calibrated.

options.text: Have the session that generated the findings re-score them a second time, and average the two scores.
options.why: This brings back the self-review bias.

options.text: Route every finding to human triage for the first year, to build trust before automating anything.
options.why: That defeats the goal and would overwhelm a 30-items-a-day queue.

questions.explanation: Per-finding confidence can drive routing, but only after calibration on labelled data.

questions.stem: The CI flow has three fixed, well-understood stages: lint-aware review, test-gap analysis, and a summary comment. Each stage consumes the previous stage's output, and the stages never change between PRs. Which pattern fits?

options.text: A coordinator agent that decides at runtime which stages each PR needs and in what order.
options.why: Adaptive decomposition adds unpredictability that a fixed pipeline doesn't need.

options.text: One prompt that performs all three stages in a single response, to minimise latency and the number of API calls.
options.why: This loses focus and makes intermediate outputs hard to validate.

options.text: Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence of focused prompts, each taking the previous stage's structured output.
options.why: Chaining suits predictable, sequential workflows.

options.text: Three parallel subagents whose outputs are merged at the end, to cut the total time of the pipeline.
options.why: The stages depend on each other, so they can't run in parallel.

questions.explanation: Use prompt chaining for fixed, known workflows and adaptive decomposition for open-ended ones.
